rationale: RF jamming and unauthenticated C2 interception are repeatable attacks that can cause loss of control and crashes, although execution requires suitable equipment and proximity or signal access.
A JWT verification bypass can grant unauthorised flight permissions repeatedly with moderate technical skill, potentially enabling widespread unsafe operations and serious airspace conflicts.

A trusted-vendor firmware compromise can distribute persistent backdoors across an entire fleet, enabling systemic loss of control, surveillance, or catastrophic flight failures despite the substantial supply-chain effort required.
Physical sabotage of critical vertiport controls can endanger aircraft and people, but requires site access and generally affects a particular facility rather than the entire U-Space ecosystem.
Audit-log manipulation can repeatedly undermine regulatory accountability across multiple USSPs, although its direct safety consequences are indirect and depend on subsequent undetected violations.
SQL injection can repeatedly expose and corrupt large volumes of flight-plan data with moderate skill, potentially disrupting coordinated operations and creating serious airspace safety risks.
Strategic document theft can expose sensitive deployment plans and defensive weaknesses, but the described disclosure has no direct safety consequence without further exploitation.

Backdoored flight-controller firmware can compromise control and safety functions across many aircraft through repeated updates, with potentially catastrophic consequences despite the technical and supply-chain access required.

Unauthenticated geofence-feed manipulation can repeatedly falsify restricted-airspace boundaries and enable dangerous incursions affecting many dependent aircraft, potentially resulting in catastrophic encounters.

Unvalidated telemetry or GNSS replay can create convincing phantom tracks and conceal real conflicts, undermining separation assurance across multiple aircraft with potentially catastrophic safety consequences.
A stolen API key and absent rate limits make bulk flight-plan exfiltration easy to repeat, exposing substantial sensitive data but causing only indirect safety consequences in the stated scenario.

Poisoning a shared single source of truth can systematically corrupt information consumed by all dependent services, producing fleet-wide coordination failures and potentially catastrophic airspace conflicts.

Weak identity proofing and stolen credentials enable repeatable impersonation and unauthorised flight approvals, potentially facilitating serious violations and unsafe operations across multiple operators.
Removing no-fly-zone boundaries through an unsecured API can repeatedly invalidate critical airspace protections for many aircraft and permit incursions with potentially catastrophic consequences.

Manipulated weather and traffic feeds can repeatedly induce unsafe routing and simultaneous traffic conflicts across multiple aircraft, with potentially catastrophic consequences depending on flight conditions.

Regulatory ambiguity can be exploited repeatedly to bypass cybersecurity obligations across multiple providers, weakening systemic resilience while producing moderate and indirect safety consequences.

GNSS spoofing or jamming can cause navigation loss and restricted-airspace deviations across multiple aircraft, potentially producing catastrophic outcomes although effective RF attacks require specialised equipment and conditions.

Tampering with audit trails can repeatedly conceal incidents and obstruct investigations across multiple systems, substantially weakening accountability but not directly causing a safety event in the stated scenario.

Ground-station outages can halt essential operations, while malicious battery-management manipulation can deplete power during flight and cause crashes, creating potentially catastrophic safety consequences.

Flooding an unprotected central API gateway is relatively easy and repeatable, potentially disabling authorisations and multiple services across an entire airspace volume and creating serious operational safety risks.

Sensor spoofing and IMU manipulation can corrupt altitude and attitude estimates, trigger unsafe flight decisions, and cause crashes, although effective attacks depend on access to relevant signals or hardware.
